title: How Schizophrenia Works
summary: Josh and Chuck explain schizophrenia: its history (Kraepelin's dementia praecox classification, Bleuler coining the name in 1911 from Greek words for split mind), common misconception vs. split personality (dissociative identity disorder), positive and negative symptoms, avolition, DSM six-month diagnostic criterion, subtypes (paranoid, disorganized/hebephrenic, catatonic, undifferentiated, residual, schizoaffective), hallucinations (mostly auditory voices, including command hallucinations and haptic hallucinations) and delusions (including delusions of reference), suicide and violence risk, recovery statistics, family communication advice, Third World recovery rates, famous people with schizophrenia (Syd Barrett, John Nash, Wesley Willis, Lionel Aldridge), causes (genetics, in utero infection, birth month effect), glutamate and dopamine research, antipsychotics and side effects, ECT, and early treatment during the prodrome. The episode closes with listener mail corrections and a sign-off.

segments.title: Opening banter and framing schizophrenia
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open with off-topic banter about Bob Dylan and David Bowie, then Josh explains why they chose schizophrenia, citing news items, misunderstanding, underfunding, and people who are homeless or incarcerated without treatment.

segments.title: History and name of schizophrenia
segments.summary: Discussion of how mental illness was viewed before the twentieth century, Emil Kraepelin's classification in the 1890s-era as a form of dementia, and Eugen Bleuler coining the name schizophrenia in 1911 from Greek words meaning split mind. They explain the split-mind name fostered a misconception that it is split personality disorder.

segments.title: Schizophrenia vs. split personality disorder
segments.summary: The hosts distinguish schizophrenia from dissociative identity disorder (split personality), noting Hollywood's fascination with multiple personalities in films and shows like The United States of Tara and Sybil.

segments.title: Onset, age, and risk
segments.summary: Schizophrenia typically develops in late teens or early twenties for men and mid twenties to early thirties for women, can come on gradually or suddenly, and has about a one percent general population prevalence. Early treatment is believed to improve outcomes.

segments.title: Positive, negative, and cognitive symptoms; avolition
segments.summary: Explanation of positive symptoms as exaggerations of normal behavior and negative symptoms as absences of normal behavior, including flat affect, cognitive deficits in attention and memory, and avolition described by Kraepelin as annihilation of the will.

segments.title: Diagnosis criteria and subtypes
segments.summary: DSM diagnostic requirement of symptoms for six months, the schizophreniform shorter form, and subtypes: paranoid, disorganized (hypophrenic), catatonic, undifferentiated, residual, and schizoaffective disorder.

segments.title: Hallucinations and delusions
segments.summary: Definitions of delusions and hallucinations. Auditory hallucinations, usually voices, are most common, sometimes arguing or commenting; command hallucinations can urge harmful acts, though most people resist them. Haptic hallucinations and delusions of reference are described.

segments.title: Outcomes, suicide, violence, and talking with patients
segments.summary: After ten years, about seventy percent improve or recover, about ten percent die, at least ten percent by suicide. Violence is linked to pre-existing violence and substance abuse. NIMH advice on responding to delusions without agreeing or arguing. Recovery rates in developing nations are reportedly higher.

segments.title: Famous people with schizophrenia
segments.summary: Discussion of Syd Barrett of Pink Floyd, John Nash of A Beautiful Mind, the disputed Navy discharge of Jack Kerouac, Pops Benny's death, musician Wesley Willis, and Green Bay Packer Lionel Aldridge who later spoke publicly about mental illness.

segments.title: Causes: genetics and infection hypotheses
segments.summary: Genes such as DISC1, dysbindin, and neuregulin are linked, with possibly a dozen more. Environmental hypotheses include in utero exposure to influenza or Toxoplasma gondii, the birth month effect, inflamed white blood cells, and a dormant retrovirus.

segments.title: Brain research and treatments
segments.summary: Research on the ventral striatum and reward prediction, the role of glutamate discovered through PCP studies leading to atypical antipsychotics, side effects of antipsychotics, electroconvulsive therapy use, and family therapy and small goal setting.

segments.title: Prodrome and early treatment
segments.summary: The prodrome period before full symptoms, and an British doctor's late-1980s program in two towns outside London using therapy and low-dose antipsychotics that reportedly reduced prevalence to a tenth of the national rate in four years. Clinics and university departments now focus on prodrome.

segments.title: Resources and sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts recommend schizophrenia resources, a Harper's article by Rachel Aviv, and a Wesley Willis documentary. They mention a closing correction segment and sign off.

segments.title: Listener mail and corrections
segments.summary: Corrections include the flash point of books (Fahrenheit 451 vs Celsius 233), the first execution in Jamestown (Billington, with a note about an earlier European executed), wildfires in South Georgia, a Hindu listener's correction on Brahman and karma, and a dispute over the pronunciation of Jainism.
